title: India Just Found Natural Gas Off the Andaman Islands. It Changes the Hormuz Calculus.
excerpt: Oil India's third exploratory well in the Andaman offshore block confirms hydrocarbon presence for the second time. With the Strait of Hormuz still choked, India's frontier basin exploration has become a strategic imperative.
body:
State-owned Oil India Limited on Friday announced a fresh discovery of natural gas in its third exploratory well in the Andaman shallow offshore block — the second confirmed hydrocarbon find in a basin that geologists have long considered one of India's most promising but least explored frontier regions.

The timing could not be more significant. India imports roughly 85 percent of its crude oil and 50 percent of its natural gas. The Strait of Hormuz — through which 40 percent of India's oil imports pass — remains severely disrupted by the Iran conflict, with traffic far below pre-war levels even months after the April ceasefire. Every barrel discovered closer to home rewrites a line in India's energy security ledger.

What Oil India Found

The Vijayapuram-3 well, drilled 15 kilometres off the east coast of the Andaman Islands at a water depth of 355 metres, struck gas at a depth of over 1,900 metres in the Eocene formation. Initial production testing confirmed the presence of natural gas through continuous flaring and immediate pressure build-up followed by gas production.

Union Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri announced the discovery on social media, describing it as "an ocean of energy opportunities reinforced in the Andaman Sea."

Oil India said gas sampling is underway to assess composition and calorific value, along with isotope studies to determine the origin of the hydrocarbons. The company's regulatory filing noted that two of the three exploratory wells drilled so far in Block AN-OSHP-2018/1 have now indicated hydrocarbon presence — a strike rate that has caught the attention of global energy majors.

The Andaman Basin's Untapped Potential

The Andaman basin sits in a geological sweet spot. Its subsurface formations share structural similarities with the proven hydrocarbon provinces of Myanmar and Indonesia, where offshore exploration has yielded commercially viable gas fields. Despite this geological promise, the Andaman basin has seen minimal exploration — a function of its remoteness, deep waters, and the logistical challenges of operating hundreds of kilometres from India's eastern seaboard.

That calculus is changing. Under the Samudra Manthan Mission — the National Deep Water Exploration Mission announced by Prime Minister Modi on Independence Day 2025 — India has planned a large number of deepwater and ultra-deepwater wells across its offshore basins. The Andaman campaign is a flagship component.

Puri noted that the discovery "will help us in taking forward our exploration ambitions in coordination with global deepwater exploration experts like Petrobras, TotalEnergies, BP India, Shell and ExxonMobil." The involvement of these companies — each with decades of deepwater experience — signals that India is serious about commercialising what the Andaman basin holds.

The Hormuz Factor

The strategic context cannot be overstated. The 2026 Iran war caused what the International Energy Agency has called "the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market." The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 percent of global oil and significant LNG volumes pass, has seen its traffic reduced to a fraction of pre-war levels.

India, with crude stocks covering only about 25 days of demand, is acutely vulnerable to this disruption. The country has already pivoted its sourcing — approaching the Trump administration for permission to resume Russian crude purchases, diversifying to Venezuela and African suppliers, and now accelerating exploration in its own waters.

The Andaman gas discovery does not solve India's energy deficit tomorrow. Gas sampling, commercial viability assessments, and the construction of production infrastructure will take years. But it adds a domestic card to a hand that has been almost entirely dependent on imports from volatile regions.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs invested in Indian energy stocks or tracking India's macroeconomic resilience, the Andaman discovery is a leading indicator. Oil India shares have been buoyant on the back of the exploration campaign. More broadly, every domestic energy discovery reduces India's current account deficit pressure, supports the rupee, and insulates the economy from external shocks — all of which affect the diaspora's financial ties to India.

The first discovery at Vijayapuram-2 came in September 2025. The second, at Vijayapuram-3, came nine months later. If the geological promise of the Andaman basin holds, the third well — or the next campaign — could be the one that moves the needle from exploratory to commercial. India's energy map is being redrawn, one well at a time.
